questions.q: What are materials and energy sources obtained from nature and used by humans called?
questions.explain: Natural resources are the materials, organisms and energy sources provided by nature that people use to meet their needs. Air, water, soil, minerals and forests all belong to this group.
why_wrong: Man-made resources are manufactured by humans, not obtained directly from nature.
Synthetic resources are produced artificially in laboratories or factories.
Industrial resources is a loose term for factory inputs, not the name for what nature provides.

questions.q: Which of the following is a biotic natural resource?
questions.explain: Biotic resources come from the living world, and forests are made of living organisms. Minerals, sunlight and water are non-living.
why_wrong: Minerals are non-living and therefore abiotic.
Sunlight is a non-living energy source and therefore abiotic.
Water is a non-living physical resource and therefore abiotic.

questions.q: Which of these is an abiotic natural resource?
questions.explain: Abiotic resources are non-living components of the environment such as minerals, air, water and sunlight. Soil minerals are non-living.
why_wrong: Fish are living organisms, so they are biotic.
Timber is obtained from living trees, so it is biotic.
Wheat is a living crop plant, so it is biotic.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a natural resource?
questions.explain: A computer is manufactured by humans from processed materials. Groundwater, sunlight and soil are provided directly by nature.
why_wrong: Groundwater occurs naturally underground and is a natural resource.
Sunlight is a naturally occurring energy resource.
Fertile soil forms naturally and is a basic natural resource.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the aim of sustainable use of natural resources?
options: Using every resource as fast as possible for economic growth
Stopping all use of natural resources completely
Using only imported resources and saving local ones for export
Meeting today's needs without harming future generations' needs
questions.explain: Sustainable use means using resources in a way that lets future generations meet their own needs too. This is the standard definition of sustainable development.
why_wrong: Rapid use depletes resources and ignores future needs.
Total prohibition is neither practical nor what sustainability means.
Sustainability concerns how resources are used, not where they are sourced.

questions.q: Which factor is the most important driver of overexploitation of natural resources?
options: A steady decrease in the demand for energy
A shrinking of industries across the world
An increase in the area of protected forests
questions.explain: More people consuming more per head puts pressure on land, water, forests and energy. This growing demand is the root of overexploitation.
why_wrong: Falling demand would ease, not increase, exploitation.
Fewer industries would reduce resource use, not raise it.
Protected forests reduce exploitation.

questions.q: On what basis are natural resources classified into renewable and non-renewable?
options: Their colour and physical state at room temperature
Their rate of replenishment compared with the rate of use
The country or region in which they are found
Whether they are bought and sold in markets
questions.explain: A resource is renewable if nature can replenish it at least as fast as it is used, and non-renewable if replenishment takes geological time. This is the basis of the classification.
why_wrong: Colour and state have no role in this classification.
Location does not decide whether a resource is renewable.
Market trade does not determine renewability.

questions.q: Which of the following is a renewable energy resource?
questions.explain: Solar energy is continuously supplied by the Sun and is not used up. Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels that take millions of years to form.
why_wrong: Coal is a fossil fuel and non-renewable.
Petroleum is a fossil fuel and non-renewable.
Natural gas is a fossil fuel and non-renewable.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-renewable resource?
questions.explain: Coal formed over millions of years and cannot be replaced within human timescales. Wind, biomass and sunlight are replenished naturally.
why_wrong: Wind is continuously renewed by atmospheric processes.
Biomass can be regrown within a short time.
Solar radiation is supplied continuously by the Sun.

questions.q: Fossil fuels such as coal and petroleum were formed from which of the following?
questions.explain: Over millions of years, heat and pressure acting on buried organic remains converted them into coal, oil and gas. That is why they are called fossil fuels.
why_wrong: Volcanic ash does not make fuels.
Stored rainwater is groundwater, not fuel.
Seawater salts form salt deposits, not fuels.

questions.q: Which one is the odd one out in this list?
questions.explain: Natural gas is a fossil fuel and non-renewable, while the other three are renewable. It is therefore the odd one out.
why_wrong: Wind energy is renewable like the others in the rest of the list.
Solar energy is renewable like the others in the rest of the list.
Biomass energy is renewable, so it is not the odd one out.

questions.q: Why can groundwater behave like a non-renewable resource in some regions?
options: It is chemically classed as a mineral
It is pumped out much faster than it is recharged
It cannot be used for crop irrigation
It never takes part in the water cycle at all
questions.explain: Aquifers recharge slowly through rainfall percolation. When extraction exceeds recharge for long periods, the resource is effectively mined and depleted.
why_wrong: Water is not a mineral, and the issue is the rate of use.
Groundwater is widely used for irrigation.
Groundwater is recharged through the water cycle.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched as renewable and non-renewable resources respectively?
questions.explain: Timber can be regrown by planting trees, while uranium ore is a finite mineral. The pair is therefore in the order renewable then non-renewable.
why_wrong: This reverses the correct order.
Coal is non-renewable and wind is renewable, so this order is reversed.
Petroleum is non-renewable and sunlight is renewable, so this order is reversed.

questions.q: A renewable resource like fish can effectively become non-renewable when
options: it is harvested faster than it can reproduce
it is harvested slowly and carefully
only mature fish are caught seasonally
questions.explain: Renewability depends on regeneration keeping pace with use. Overfishing can push stocks below recovery level, leading to collapse.
why_wrong: Slow, careful harvest allows regeneration.
Protecting breeding grounds supports renewal.
Seasonal harvest of mature fish allows stocks to recover.

questions.q: The removal of the fertile top layer of soil by wind or running water is called
questions.explain: Soil erosion is the wearing away and transport of top soil by wind or water. It removes the nutrient-rich layer needed for crops.
why_wrong: Soil formation is the slow build-up of soil.
Fertilisation adds nutrients to soil.
Ploughing is tilling of land by farmers.

questions.q: The process by which fertile land turns into desert-like land is called
questions.explain: Desertification is the degradation of fertile land in dry regions into desert, caused by drought, overgrazing and poor farming. It reduces productivity of the land.
why_wrong: Afforestation is planting trees on non-forest land.
Urbanisation is the growth of cities.
Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of water bodies.

questions.q: The build-up of salts in the soil due to excessive irrigation is called
questions.explain: Irrigation water contains dissolved salts, which are left behind as water evaporates, especially with poor drainage. Over time the soil becomes saline and unfit for crops.
why_wrong: Erosion is removal of soil, not accumulation of salts.
Leaching is washing of soluble nutrients down the soil.
Succession is the replacement of one community by another.

questions.q: Which farming method on hill slopes best reduces soil erosion?
options: Ploughing up and down the slope
questions.explain: Terraces convert a slope into steps that slow runoff and hold soil. This method is widely used in hilly regions.
why_wrong: Ploughing along the slope speeds up runoff and erosion.
Clearing vegetation exposes soil to erosion.
Overgrazing removes the protective plant cover.

questions.q: Rows of trees planted at the edge of fields to reduce wind erosion are called
questions.explain: Shelterbelts break the force of wind and so protect the soil and crops. They are a standard remedy for wind erosion in dry regions.
why_wrong: Terraces are steps built on slopes to control water erosion.
Check dams are small barriers across streams or gullies.
Contour bunds are earth ridges that hold water on slopes.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a cause of land degradation?
questions.explain: Planting suitable native trees protects and restores land. The other three damage soil structure and fertility.
why_wrong: Overgrazing strips vegetation and causes erosion.
Mining without restoration leaves scarred, barren land.
Excess fertilisers harm soil life and cause salinity.

questions.q: Waterlogging of agricultural land is mainly caused by
options: very low rainfall and sparse irrigation
excess irrigation combined with poor drainage
questions.explain: When too much water is applied and drainage is poor, the water table rises to the root zone. Roots then lack oxygen and crop yields fall.
why_wrong: Little water cannot cause waterlogging.
Deep ploughing alone does not raise the water table.
Deep-rooted trees lower the water table rather than raise it.

questions.q: Which sector is the largest user of fresh water worldwide?
questions.explain: Irrigation of crops takes the largest share of fresh water withdrawals globally. Domestic and industrial uses are smaller.
why_wrong: Domestic use is smaller than agricultural use.
Industry uses less than agriculture overall.
Recreation uses very little fresh water.

questions.q: An underground layer of rock or sediment that holds and yields groundwater is called
questions.explain: An aquifer stores water in its pores and fractures and can be tapped by wells. It is the main groundwater reservoir.
why_wrong: A watershed is the land area draining into a river.
A lagoon is a shallow coastal water body.
A delta is a landform at a river mouth.

questions.q: Collecting and storing rainwater for later use is known as
questions.explain: Rainwater harvesting captures rain from roofs or land and stores it or recharges groundwater. It is a key water conservation method.
why_wrong: Desalination removes salts from seawater.
Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of water bodies.
Waterlogging is saturation of soil with water.

questions.q: Heavy pumping of groundwater in excess of its recharge leads to
questions.explain: When withdrawal exceeds recharge, the level of groundwater drops and wells run dry. This is a widespread problem in parts of India.
why_wrong: A rising water table results from excess recharge.
Pumping does not alter rainfall.
Pumping has no bearing on the evaporation rate.

questions.q: Which of the following is a major social problem associated with large dams?
options: A rise in the price of cement
An increase in the area of desert
A permanent loss of all river flow
questions.explain: Reservoirs submerge villages and farmland, so people lose homes and livelihoods and need rehabilitation. This is a well-known issue of big dams.
why_wrong: Cement price is unrelated to the social problem of dams.
Dams do not increase desert area.
Dams regulate flow but do not stop the river permanently.

questions.q: The Cauvery river water dispute is mainly between which states?
questions.explain: The Cauvery dispute over sharing river water is a well-known inter-state water conflict between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. It illustrates conflicts over water resources.
why_wrong: Punjab and Haryana have disputes over the Sutlej-Yamuna link canal.
Gujarat and Rajasthan are not the parties in the Cauvery dispute.
Assam and West Bengal are not the parties in the Cauvery dispute.

questions.q: Excess fluoride in drinking water causes which health problem?
questions.explain: Long-term intake of fluoride-rich groundwater damages teeth and bones, a condition called fluorosis. It is common in parts of Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh.
why_wrong: Scurvy results from vitamin C deficiency.
Goitre results from iodine deficiency.
Rickets results from vitamin D deficiency.

questions.q: The large-scale cutting down and clearing of forests is called
questions.explain: Deforestation is the permanent removal of forest cover for timber, farming, mining or settlements. It leads to loss of biodiversity and soil.
why_wrong: Afforestation is planting trees on non-forest land.
Reforestation is replanting where forest was cut.
This is not a recognised term for clearing forests.

questions.q: Planting trees on land that was not previously forested is called
questions.explain: Afforestation creates forest in an area that had no forest cover recently. It helps restore soil and absorb carbon dioxide.
why_wrong: Deforestation is clearing of forest.
Desertification is degradation into desert.
Eutrophication concerns water bodies.

questions.q: Which gas do forests absorb from the atmosphere during photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Green plants take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen in photosynthesis. This is why forests act as carbon sinks.
why_wrong: Plants do not absorb atmospheric nitrogen for photosynthesis.
Methane is not what photosynthesis consumes.
Carbon monoxide is not used in photosynthesis.

questions.q: The Chipko movement in India was started to
questions.explain: Villagers, many of them women, hugged trees to prevent felling in the Himalayan region. It became a symbol of community forest protection.
why_wrong: Chipko opposed felling, not dam building.
Chipko opposed forest exploitation, not mining expansion.
Chipko was about forests, not city growth.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a cause of deforestation?
questions.explain: Social forestry plants trees and so restores cover. The other three clear forest land.
why_wrong: Shifting cultivation clears forests by slash and burn.
Mining operations clear forest areas.
Large dams submerge forests.

questions.q: Why does shifting (jhum) cultivation contribute to deforestation?
options: Trees are planted in every plot
Only dead wood is collected by farmers
Plots are cleared, burnt, then abandoned
Crops are grown under canopy without clearing
questions.explain: In jhum, plots are cleared by burning and abandoned when fertility falls, so new forest is cleared repeatedly. Short fallow periods prevent regrowth.
why_wrong: Planting trees would not cause deforestation.
Collecting only dead wood does not clear forest.
Growing under canopy without clearing does not remove forest.

questions.q: In Joint Forest Management (JFM), what is the role of local communities?
options: They are removed from the forest areas
They are given full ownership of all forests
They are only allowed to sell the timber
They help protect forests and share the benefits
questions.explain: JFM involves villagers with the forest department in protecting forest and sharing forest produce. It aims to link conservation with livelihood.
why_wrong: JFM involves the communities rather than removing them.
JFM does not hand over full ownership of forests.
JFM is about protection and sharing of benefits, not just timber sale.

questions.q: Energy obtained from the heat inside the Earth is called
questions.explain: Geothermal energy comes from hot rocks and steam below the surface. It is used for heating and for generating electricity.
why_wrong: Tidal energy comes from the rise and fall of the sea.
Wind energy comes from moving air.
Biogas comes from decomposing organic waste.

questions.q: Devices that convert sunlight directly into electricity are called
questions.explain: Photovoltaic or solar cells use semiconductors to turn light into electric current. They are the basis of solar panels.
why_wrong: Fuel cells convert chemical energy of a fuel.
Dry cells store chemical energy.
Dynamos convert mechanical energy to electricity.

questions.q: The main constituent of biogas and natural gas is
questions.explain: Methane (CH4) makes up the bulk of both natural gas and biogas. It burns with a clean flame.
why_wrong: Oxygen is not a fuel gas.
Hydrogen sulphide is only a minor impurity.
Carbon monoxide is not a main component.

questions.q: Which element is the main fuel used in nuclear power plants?
questions.explain: Uranium-235 undergoes fission and releases large amounts of heat used to make steam. It is the chief nuclear fuel.
why_wrong: Sulphur is not a nuclear fuel.
Copper is a conductor, not a nuclear fuel.
Calcium is not a nuclear fuel.

questions.q: Which is a main drawback of nuclear energy?
options: Emission of large amounts of soot
questions.explain: Spent nuclear fuel stays radioactive for a very long time and needs safe storage. Nuclear plants also carry accident risk.
why_wrong: Soot is a problem of coal, not of nuclear power.
Nuclear plants do not depend on rainfall for fuel.
Wind speed is relevant to wind power, not nuclear.

questions.q: Biogas is produced mainly by which process?
options: Burning of dry wood in a stove
questions.explain: Microbes digest organic matter in the absence of oxygen and release methane-rich gas. Gobar gas plants in Indian villages use this process.
why_wrong: Burning wood gives heat and smoke, not biogas.
Petroleum compression gives no biogas.
Nuclear fission is unrelated to biogas.

questions.q: Which one is the odd one out among the following energy sources?
questions.explain: Nuclear fission uses limited uranium and is classed as non-renewable, while the others are renewable. It is therefore the odd one out.
why_wrong: Tidal energy is renewable like the rest of the list.
Wind energy is renewable like the rest of the list.
Geothermal energy is renewable, so it is not the odd one.

questions.q: What do the three R's of waste management stand for?
questions.explain: The three R's are Reduce, Reuse and Recycle, a basic guide to lowering waste. Individuals can apply them in daily life.
why_wrong: Remove, Recover and Rebuild are not the accepted three R's of waste management.
Reject, Repair and Resell is not the standard three R's formula.
Refill, Rebuild and Return is not the standard three R's formula.

questions.q: Which habit helps an individual conserve water?
options: Washing the car daily with a hose
Closing the tap while brushing teeth
questions.explain: Turning off the tap when not needed saves many litres a day. Small habits add up when practised by many people.
why_wrong: Daily hose washing wastes a lot of water.
Dripping taps waste water.
Half loads waste water and energy.

questions.q: Switching off unused lights and fans helps to
questions.explain: Using less electricity reduces the fossil fuel burnt at power stations. It also lowers the bill.
why_wrong: Saving energy reduces pollution.
Saving energy reduces fuel use.
Saving energy lowers bills.

questions.q: Which individual action most directly cuts fossil fuel use in daily travel?
options: Idling the engine at red lights
questions.explain: Sharing rides or using public transport means fewer vehicles burn fuel for the same journeys. It also lowers emissions.
why_wrong: A second car increases fuel use.
Idling wastes fuel.
Solo short trips use more fuel per person.

questions.q: In the waste hierarchy, which of the three R's is given the highest priority?
questions.explain: Reducing consumption prevents waste at the source and saves the most resources. Reuse comes next, and recycling, which needs energy, comes last.
why_wrong: Reuse is the second priority.
Recycling is the third priority and needs energy.
The three R's are ranked, with reduce first.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a good conservation practice?
options: Carrying a cloth bag for shopping
Repairing old items instead of discarding
Using single-use plastic and throwing it away
Refilling a reusable water bottle daily
questions.explain: Single-use plastic wastes resources and creates long-lasting waste. The other practices follow reduce and reuse.
why_wrong: Cloth bags reduce plastic use.
Repairing extends the life of goods.
Refilling reduces bottle waste.

questions.q: Composting kitchen waste at home helps conservation mainly by
options: returning nutrients to soil and cutting landfill waste
producing plastic that can be reused at home
increasing the use of chemical fertilisers in gardens
adding to the total volume of household garbage
questions.explain: Compost enriches soil with nutrients and diverts wet waste from landfills. It supports soil conservation.
why_wrong: Composting does not produce plastic.
Compost reduces the need for chemical fertilisers.
Composting reduces garbage volume.

questions.q: Who coined the term 'ecosystem'?
questions.explain: Arthur G. Tansley introduced the term ecosystem in 1935. It describes living organisms and their physical environment acting together.
why_wrong: Charles Elton is known for food chains and pyramids.
Ernst Haeckel coined the term ecology.
Eugene Odum is known as a pioneer of ecosystem ecology but did not coin the term.

questions.q: Which organisms form the producers of an ecosystem?
questions.explain: Green plants and algae make food by photosynthesis and so are the producers. All other organisms depend on them.
why_wrong: Herbivores are consumers.
Carnivores are consumers.
Decomposing bacteria are decomposers, not the producers.

questions.q: Which organisms break down dead organic matter in an ecosystem?
questions.explain: Bacteria and fungi decompose dead matter and release nutrients back into the soil. They complete nutrient recycling.
why_wrong: Producers make food from sunlight.
Primary consumers eat plants.
Secondary consumers eat herbivores.

questions.q: Which of the following is a functional aspect, not a structural component, of an ecosystem?
questions.explain: Structure refers to the components present, while function refers to processes such as energy flow and nutrient cycling. Energy flow is a function.
why_wrong: Producers are a biotic structural component.
Decomposers are a biotic structural component.
Soil and water are abiotic structural components.

questions.q: In the chain grass, grasshopper, frog, the frog is a
questions.explain: The grasshopper eats grass and is the primary consumer, so the frog that eats it is a secondary consumer. Position depends on what the organism eats.
why_wrong: Producers are plants.
The primary consumer here is the grasshopper.
A decomposer feeds on dead matter, which a frog catching prey does not.

questions.q: Which organism is a detritivore?
questions.explain: Earthworms ingest and fragment dead organic matter, making it easier for decomposers to act. Mushrooms and bacteria decompose chemically.
why_wrong: Mushrooms are fungal decomposers.
Rhizobium is a nitrogen-fixing bacterium.
Bacillus is a decomposing bacterium.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an abiotic component of an ecosystem?
questions.explain: Fungi are living organisms and so are biotic. Temperature, soil and sunlight are non-living factors.
why_wrong: Temperature is abiotic.
Soil is abiotic.
Sunlight is abiotic.

questions.q: Camels and cacti are typically found in which ecosystem?
questions.explain: Both are adapted to scarce water and high temperatures of a desert. Camels store fat and cacti store water.
why_wrong: An estuary is a water-rich river mouth.
Coral reefs are marine ecosystems.
Mangroves grow in tidal coasts.

questions.q: A pond is an example of which type of ecosystem?
questions.explain: A pond is a small body of fresh water and its organisms, which makes it a freshwater aquatic ecosystem.
why_wrong: Terrestrial ecosystems are on land.
A pond is not a desert.
Grasslands are land ecosystems.

questions.q: The partly enclosed area where a river meets the sea and fresh water mixes with salt water is called
questions.explain: Estuaries have brackish water and are productive nursery grounds for many fish.
why_wrong: Tundra is a cold treeless biome.
An oasis is a desert water source.
Savanna is a tropical grassland.

questions.q: A crop field is an example of which kind of ecosystem?
questions.explain: Humans design and maintain crop fields, so they are artificial ecosystems.
why_wrong: Forests are natural.
Marine ecosystems are in oceans.
Polar ecosystems are cold natural regions.

questions.q: Which one is the odd one out?
questions.explain: Desert is a terrestrial ecosystem while the others are freshwater aquatic ecosystems.
why_wrong: Pond is aquatic.
Lake is aquatic.
River is aquatic.

questions.q: Which of the following is a lotic (flowing water) ecosystem?
questions.explain: Lotic systems have moving water, as in rivers and streams. Ponds and lakes are lentic (still water).
why_wrong: Ponds are still water.
Lakes are still water.
Swamp pools are still water.

questions.q: Which ecosystem is characterised by permafrost and a short growing season?
questions.explain: Tundra has a permanently frozen subsoil called permafrost and mostly mosses and lichens.
why_wrong: Rainforests are warm and wet.
Savannas are warm grasslands.
Mangroves are tropical coasts.

questions.q: What is the ultimate source of energy for almost all ecosystems?
questions.explain: Producers capture solar energy by photosynthesis, supporting all other organisms.
why_wrong: Wind is not a source of energy for living things.
Soil is a nutrient source, not an energy source.
Water is not an energy source for organisms.

questions.q: Energy flow in an ecosystem is
questions.explain: Energy moves one way from the Sun to producers to consumers and is lost as heat. It cannot be reused.
why_wrong: Nutrients, not energy, cycle.
Energy does not flow back.
Energy flow follows trophic levels.

questions.q: According to Lindeman's ten percent law, how much energy passes from one trophic level to the next?
questions.explain: Roughly one tenth of energy is stored at the next level, the rest is lost.
why_wrong: 90 percent is the amount lost.
50 percent is far too high.
100 percent would mean no loss.

questions.q: Most energy at each trophic level is lost mainly as heat through
questions.explain: Organisms use energy in metabolism, releasing heat. Hence little is left for the next level.
why_wrong: Photosynthesis captures energy.
Transpiration is water loss from plants.
Pollination is transfer of pollen.

questions.q: Why do food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels?
options: Plants cannot grow beyond four or five levels
Too little energy remains after repeated losses
Carnivores refuse to eat other carnivores
Sunlight stops reaching the Earth's surface
questions.explain: Because only about 10 percent passes on, little energy remains at the top.
why_wrong: Plants do not set the limit.
Carnivores can eat each other; energy is the limit.
Sunlight continues to reach Earth.

questions.q: If producers store 10000 J of energy, how much is available to secondary consumers by the ten percent law?
questions.explain: Producers to primary consumers gives 1000 J, then to secondary consumers 100 J.
why_wrong: 1000 J reaches primary consumers.
10 J would be the tertiary level.
5000 J ignores the law.

questions.q: Which statement about energy and nutrients in an ecosystem is correct?
options: Nutrients are recycled whereas energy flows one way
Energy is recycled but nutrients flow one way
questions.explain: Matter cycles between organisms and the environment, but energy is lost as heat.
why_wrong: Energy is not recycled.
It is nutrients that cycle.
Both move between organisms.

questions.q: A series of organisms in which each eats the one before it is called a
questions.explain: A food chain shows a linear transfer of energy from producers to consumers.
why_wrong: Pyramids show numbers, biomass or energy.
A web is many interlinked chains.
Food cycle is not the standard term.

questions.q: A network of many interconnected food chains is called a
questions.explain: Most organisms eat several foods, so chains interlink to form a web.
why_wrong: A chain is a single line.
Trophic cycle is not the standard term.
A biome is a large ecological region.

questions.q: Each step of a food chain is called a
questions.explain: Producers form the first trophic level, herbivores the second, and so on.
why_wrong: A niche is the role of a species.
A habitat is a place.
A community is all populations in an area.

questions.q: In grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, which organism is the tertiary consumer?
questions.explain: Grass is the producer, grasshopper the primary, frog the secondary and snake the tertiary consumer.
why_wrong: Grass is the producer.
Grasshopper is the primary consumer.
Frog is the secondary consumer.

questions.q: Which of the following is a detritus food chain?
questions.explain: A detritus food chain begins with dead organic matter.
why_wrong: Begins with living grass, so it is a grazing chain.
Begins with living phytoplankton, so it is grazing.
Begins with living grass, so it is grazing.

questions.q: Why is a food web more stable than a single food chain?
options: It has fewer organisms in total
Consumers have alternative foods if one is lost
It contains only producers and no consumers
It has a single path for energy flow
questions.explain: With many alternative paths, loss of one species does not collapse the system.
why_wrong: Webs have more, not fewer, organisms.
Webs include consumers.
A single path makes a chain fragile.

questions.q: Which organism is likely to carry the highest DDT concentration in a food chain?
options: The grass growing in the field
A top carnivore such as an eagle
questions.explain: DDT is not broken down and builds up at higher trophic levels, called biomagnification.
why_wrong: Producers have the lowest concentration.
Herbivores carry less than top carnivores.
Producers have the lowest concentration.

questions.q: The ecological pyramid concept was introduced by
questions.explain: Charles Elton described pyramids of numbers in 1927.
why_wrong: Lindeman gave the ten percent law.
Tansley coined the term ecosystem.
Odum popularised ecosystem ecology.

questions.q: What is placed at the base of an ecological pyramid?
questions.explain: Producers support all higher trophic levels, so form the base.
why_wrong: Decomposers are not placed at the base.
Top carnivores occupy the apex.
Herbivores are the second level.

questions.q: Which ecological pyramid is always upright?
questions.explain: Energy decreases at each level because of losses, so the pyramid is always upright.
why_wrong: Numbers can be inverted.
Biomass can be inverted in aquatic systems.
Pyramid of age is not one of the standard pyramids.

questions.q: The pyramid of numbers is inverted in which ecosystem?
questions.explain: One large tree supports many insects, so the top level has more individuals.
why_wrong: Grassland pyramid of numbers is upright.
Pond is the standard example for biomass.
Desert is not the standard example.

questions.q: The pyramid of biomass is typically inverted in which ecosystem?
questions.explain: Phytoplankton have small biomass but reproduce rapidly, so zooplankton and fish can outweigh them.
why_wrong: Grassland biomass is upright.
Forest biomass is upright.
Cropland biomass is upright.

questions.q: Why is the pyramid of energy always upright?
options: Energy is added at each level
Energy is lost at each trophic level
questions.explain: As energy is lost as heat, each level has less than the one below.
why_wrong: Number of organisms does not decide it.
Energy is not added at each level.
Consumers do not produce energy.

questions.q: Which two pyramids can be inverted in some ecosystems?
questions.explain: Numbers and biomass can be inverted, but energy never.
why_wrong: The energy pyramid is never inverted, so this pair is wrong.
The energy pyramid is never inverted, so naming it alone is wrong.
The energy pyramid is never inverted, so this pair is wrong.

questions.q: The gradual and orderly replacement of one community by another is called
questions.explain: Succession is the sequential change in community until a stable stage is reached.
why_wrong: Biomagnification is the build-up of toxins.
Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment.
Adaptive radiation is evolutionary diversification.

questions.q: The first species to colonise a bare area are called
questions.explain: Pioneers such as lichens start succession.
why_wrong: Climax species belong to the final stage.
Keystone species have large effects on community.
Endemic species are restricted to a region.

questions.q: The final, stable community of a succession is called the
questions.explain: The climax community is in balance with the environment.
why_wrong: Pioneer is the first stage.
Seral communities are the intermediate stages.
An edge community lies at habitat boundaries.

questions.q: Primary succession begins on
questions.explain: No soil exists at the start, so it proceeds slowly.
why_wrong: Abandoned farmland has soil, so succession is secondary.
Burnt forest has soil, so secondary.
Cleared forest with soil leads to secondary.

questions.q: Which organisms are usually the pioneers on bare rock?
questions.explain: Lichens secrete acids that break the rock and help form soil.
why_wrong: Trees come at a late stage.
Grasses follow after soil forms.
Shrubs come after grasses.

questions.q: Why is secondary succession usually faster than primary succession?
options: No organisms exist at the start
Soil and seeds are already present
It needs no sunlight at all
questions.explain: Soil with seed bank allows rapid regrowth.
why_wrong: Succession needs organisms to begin.
Bare rock marks primary succession.
Sunlight is needed.

questions.q: A village in Rajasthan pumps groundwater much faster than rainfall recharges the aquifer. How is the groundwater best described?
options: A non-renewable resource, because groundwater can never be replenished by rain
An inexhaustible resource, because rain falls every year
A fossil resource formed over millions of years
A renewable resource being used beyond its replenishment rate
questions.explain: Groundwater is renewable because the water cycle recharges it, but it is exhaustible when withdrawal exceeds recharge. Renewability depends on the rate of use versus the rate of renewal.
why_wrong: Groundwater is recharged by rain and seepage, so it is renewable in principle.
Rain is variable and recharge is limited, so the supply is not inexhaustible.
Groundwater is not a fossil fuel and is not formed over geological ages.

questions.q: A state plans to base its electricity on coal for the next century. Which property of coal makes this plan unsustainable?
options: It forms over millions of years, far slower than it is consumed
It is formed only in tropical regions and is quickly replaced there by new swamps
It cannot be burnt without water
It is produced only from living animals
questions.explain: Coal formed from buried plant matter over geological time, so its formation rate is negligible against consumption. This is what defines a non-renewable resource.
why_wrong: Coal occurs in many regions, and location does not decide renewability.
Coal burns in air and needs no water for combustion.
Coal arises mainly from buried plant matter, not from animals.

questions.q: Farmers on steep hill slopes in Uttarakhand lose topsoil every monsoon. Which measure best reduces this loss?
options: Ploughing straight up and down the slope and leaving the furrows open
Clearing the remaining trees for more fields
Building terraces and planting vegetation cover
Leaving the soil bare after harvest
questions.explain: Terraces break the slope and slow runoff, and plant roots bind the soil. Together they reduce erosion on steep land.
why_wrong: Ploughing along the slope direction channels water and speeds erosion.
Removing trees removes the roots that hold soil.
Bare soil is exposed to raindrop impact and runoff.

questions.q: After years of canal irrigation, a farm in Punjab shows a white salt crust on the surface and falling crop yield. Which problem and remedy match?
options: Desertification of dry land; plant more shelterbelts and reduce all irrigation
Salinisation and waterlogging; improve drainage and use salt-tolerant crops
Soil erosion by wind; add more canal water
questions.explain: Excess irrigation with poor drainage raises the water table and brings salts to the surface. Drainage and tolerant crops are the standard remedies.
why_wrong: Desertification involves loss of vegetation in dry areas, and shelterbelts do not remove salts.
More water would worsen waterlogging and salt build-up.
Landslides occur on slopes, not on flat irrigated fields.

questions.q: Goats and cattle graze a dry rangeland in western India all year, leaving little vegetation and loose soil. Which is the most suitable remedy?
options: Controlled, rotational grazing with planted grasses and shelterbelts
Increasing the herd size so that all the available grass is used up each year
Burning the remaining grass to speed regrowth
Ploughing the land to plant a single crop
questions.explain: Overgrazing strips cover and invites erosion and desertification. Regulating grazing and restoring cover lets the land recover.
why_wrong: More animals would intensify the damage.
Burning removes the remaining cover and exposes soil.
Ploughing dry loose land increases wind erosion.

questions.q: An opencast coal mine in Jharkhand has left deep pits and barren heaps of overburden. Which step is the correct remedial measure?
options: Abandon the site completely so that nature heals it unaided in a few seasons
Fill the pits with industrial effluent
Build houses directly on the loose overburden
Backfill the pits and reclaim the land by afforestation
questions.explain: Mine reclamation restores the land through backfilling, levelling and planting. This reduces erosion and returns the land to productive use.
why_wrong: Abandoned spoil heaps stay barren and keep eroding for decades.
Effluent would pollute soil and groundwater.
Loose overburden is unstable for construction.

questions.q: The water table in a growing city falls every year while paved area increases. Which intervention directly targets this problem?
options: Drilling deeper borewells to reach older water below the falling water table
Rainwater harvesting with recharge pits and permeable surfaces
questions.explain: Recharge structures let rain percolate into the aquifer and offset withdrawal. Deeper borewells only speed up depletion.
why_wrong: Deeper wells lower the table further and do not add water.
Concrete prevents infiltration and reduces recharge.
Bottled water does not restore the aquifer.

questions.q: A big dam on a river submerges several tribal villages and their farmland. Which problem is this?
options: Salt build-up in the reservoir water because of continuous evaporation
Displacement of people and the need for rehabilitation
questions.explain: Submergence forces families to relocate, which is a major social problem of large dams. Compensation and rehabilitation are often inadequate.
why_wrong: Reservoir salinity is not the problem described here.
Dams trap silt, so downstream silt actually falls.
Ozone depletion is caused by CFCs, not dams.

questions.q: In a coastal town, heavy groundwater pumping leaves wells yielding salty water. What has most likely happened?
options: Rainwater has dissolved the topsoil and washed its salts into the wells
The wells have been recharged too much
The river has deposited extra silt
Seawater has intruded into the depleted freshwater aquifer
questions.explain: Over-extraction lowers freshwater pressure in coastal aquifers, letting seawater move inland. The wells then draw saline water.
why_wrong: Rain recharges freshwater and does not salinate wells.
Too much recharge would dilute, not salinate, the water.
Silt deposits do not make groundwater salty.

questions.q: After heavy rain, a river floods a valley whose upstream hills were recently deforested. Why did deforestation worsen the flood?
options: Less infiltration and more surface runoff reached the river quickly
Trees normally add extra water to the river through their roots during storms
Roots increase the speed of surface flow
questions.explain: Forest litter and roots absorb rain and slow runoff. Without them, more water reaches the river fast and the peak flow is higher.
why_wrong: Trees do not add water to rivers; they hold and release it slowly.
Roots slow flow and hold soil.
Reduced infiltration lowers groundwater storage.

questions.q: Villagers drinking from tubewells in parts of West Bengal develop skin lesions over years. Which groundwater contaminant is most commonly responsible?
questions.explain: Arsenic occurs naturally in some alluvial aquifers of the Ganga delta. Long-term intake causes skin lesions and other disease.
why_wrong: Chlorine is added to disinfect water and does not cause such lesions.
Dissolved oxygen is harmless.
Calcium carbonate causes hardness, not skin lesions.

questions.q: Village women hug trees to stop a contractor from felling them. Which movement does this describe?
questions.explain: Chipko began in the Himalayan region of Uttarakhand as a non-violent protest where villagers embraced trees. It is a well-known example of community action for forests.
why_wrong: Narmada Bachao Andolan opposed big dams on the Narmada.
Silent Valley concerned a hydroelectric project in Kerala.
The Green Revolution was about high-yield crop varieties.

questions.q: A new highway cuts through a continuous forest and splits it into two blocks. Which is the most direct ecological consequence?
options: Habitat fragmentation that isolates animal populations
Increase in the total forest area because of the new road corridor
questions.explain: Roads divide habitats and restrict movement and gene flow. Smaller isolated patches support fewer and weaker populations.
why_wrong: Clearing a road reduces, not increases, forest area.
Ozone formation is unrelated to forest fragmentation.
Reducing forest cover tends to lower recharge.

questions.q: Tribal farmers in the north-east shorten the fallow period of jhum cultivation from many years to two. What is the likely result?
options: Soil becomes more fertile with each cycle because ash is added repeatedly
Soil fertility and forest regrowth cannot recover between cycles
questions.explain: Shifting cultivation is sustainable only with long fallows. Short cycles exhaust the soil and prevent regrowth, causing degradation.
why_wrong: Shorter fallow gives less time for nutrients to rebuild.
Less regrowth time reduces forest recovery.
Repeated clearing reduces species.

questions.q: A state forest department lets villagers collect fuelwood and minor produce in return for protecting the forest. What is this arrangement called?
options: Clear felling, where all trees of an area are cut at one time
Social distancing between forest guards and nearby village residents
Monoculture plantation of a single timber species
questions.explain: Joint Forest Management involves local communities in protecting forests and shares benefits with them. It links livelihood with conservation.
why_wrong: Clear felling removes all trees in an area.
Social distancing is unrelated to forest management.
Monoculture plantation means growing a single species.

questions.q: A household replaces all its incandescent bulbs with LED bulbs. Which conservation principle does this show?
options: Switching over to a non-renewable source of electricity at the power station
Improving energy efficiency to cut demand
questions.explain: LEDs give the same light for much less electricity. Using less energy for the same service reduces fuel burnt at power stations.
why_wrong: LEDs do not change the source type of the grid.
Lower demand reduces fossil fuel use.
Nuclear waste is not an energy storage method.

questions.q: A remote farming village has plenty of cattle dung but no grid supply. Which energy option best suits it?
questions.explain: Biogas plants digest dung anaerobically to give methane-rich fuel and nutrient-rich slurry. They suit rural areas with livestock.
why_wrong: A coal plant needs mined coal and transport infrastructure.
Reactors are unsuitable for small isolated villages.
Offshore wind needs a sea coast and a grid link, which a remote farming village lacks.

questions.q: A desert region with strong sunlight and large barren land plans a power plant. Which choice is the best fit?
options: A solar photovoltaic or solar thermal plant
A geothermal plant that runs on energy from the sea waves
A hydroelectric dam without any river
questions.explain: Deserts have high solar radiation and ample low-value land. Solar plants emit no greenhouse gases during operation.
why_wrong: Tidal power requires a coast with strong tides.
Sea waves are not a geothermal source.
A dam requires a river and a reservoir.

questions.q: A country expands nuclear power to cut carbon emissions. Which problem still needs a long-term solution?
options: Emission of large amounts of carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Nuclear plants emit little CO2 in operation but produce long-lived radioactive waste. Its safe storage remains a major challenge.
why_wrong: Nuclear generation does not burn fuel to emit CO2.
Nuclear plants do not use coal.
Acid rain comes mainly from fossil fuel burning.

questions.q: A college canteen throws away thousands of plastic cups daily. Which action should come first in the 3R order of priority?
options: Recycle the cups after they are dumped together with other waste
Reduce use by shifting to steel tumblers
Reuse by melting for road tar
questions.explain: The 3R hierarchy places reduce first, then reuse, then recycle. Preventing waste is more effective than managing it later.
why_wrong: Recycling is the last of the three and still consumes energy.
Melting for road tar is a later-stage handling step, not prevention.
Dumping into a drain pollutes and is not a conservation action.

questions.q: A student collects kitchen peels and garden leaves into a pit to make compost for her plants. Which two conservation goals does this serve?
options: Reducing waste and returning nutrients to the soil
Increasing landfill load and also raising the salinity of the soil
Raising fossil fuel use and air pollution
questions.explain: Composting diverts organic waste from landfill and returns nutrients and organic matter to the soil. It improves soil structure and water retention.
why_wrong: Composting lowers landfill load and does not salinate soil.
Compost improves soil life and water retention.
Composting uses no fossil fuel.

questions.q: Fungi grow on a dead fish lying at the edge of a pond. In ecosystem terms, what is the role of the fungi?
options: Producers that fix carbon dioxide using energy from sunlight
Decomposers that break down dead organic matter
questions.explain: Fungi secrete enzymes that digest dead matter and release nutrients back to the environment. They are saprotrophic decomposers.
why_wrong: Fungi lack chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise.
They feed on dead matter, not on living algae.
Fungi are living, so they are biotic.

questions.q: In a grassland, the total energy fixed by plants is 1000 units and plants use 400 units in respiration. What is the net primary production?
questions.explain: Net primary production equals gross primary production minus respiration loss. Here 1000 - 400 = 600 units, which is available to consumers.
why_wrong: Adding respiration to GPP is incorrect.
400 units is the respiration loss, not the net production.
1000 units is the gross production before respiration.

questions.q: A wheat field in Haryana is ploughed, sown, irrigated and harvested by farmers. How is this ecosystem classified?
options: An artificial ecosystem maintained by humans
A self-regulating natural climax ecosystem needing no human input
questions.explain: Crop fields are man-made and depend on human inputs such as seeds, water and fertiliser. They do not self-regulate like natural ecosystems.
why_wrong: A wheat field is a terrestrial system.
It has no forest structure.
It would not persist without continuous human management.

questions.q: The Sundarbans lie where rivers meet the Bay of Bengal, with fluctuating salinity and salt-tolerant trees. Which ecosystem type is this?
options: Hot desert ecosystem with very little water
Freshwater pond ecosystem with no tides at all
questions.explain: Mangroves grow in tidal estuaries where fresh and sea water mix. The Sundarbans is a classic Indian example.
why_wrong: Deserts are dry with little water.
Tundra is cold and treeless.
Pond water is still freshwater without tidal salinity.

questions.q: In a large lake, a fish lives in the open water far from shore where sunlight penetrates. Which zone is this?
questions.explain: The limnetic zone is the open, well-lit water away from the shore. The littoral zone is shallow near the shore, the profundal is deep and dark, and the benthic is the bottom.
why_wrong: The littoral zone is near the shore.
The profundal zone is deep and lacks light.
The benthic zone is the lake bottom.

questions.q: In the chain grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, the grass holds 10000 J. Applying the ten percent law, how much energy reaches the snake?
questions.explain: Each transfer keeps about 10 percent: grass 10000, grasshopper 1000, frog 100, snake 10 J. The snake is the third consumer.
why_wrong: 1000 J is the energy at the grasshopper.
100 J is the energy at the frog.
That would be one step too many.

questions.q: A naturalist notes that no food chain in a forest has more than five links. What best explains this?
options: Predators dislike eating other predators, so chains simply stop there by choice
Large energy loss at each trophic level leaves too little for further levels
Sunlight is absent at higher levels
Decomposers eat the top predators first
questions.explain: Only about ten percent of energy passes on, so after a few steps the amount left cannot support another level.
why_wrong: Feeding behaviour is not the limit on chain length.
Sunlight is needed only by producers.
Decomposers act on dead matter and do not limit chain length.

questions.q: Dead leaves on a forest floor are eaten by earthworms, which are eaten by birds. What kind of food chain is this?
questions.explain: A detritus chain starts from dead organic matter rather than living producers. Earthworms are detritivores feeding on it.
why_wrong: A grazing chain begins with living green plants.
A parasitic chain depends on host organisms.
There is no such standard chain type.

questions.q: In a field, insects are eaten by frogs and frogs by snakes. If snakes are removed by hunting, what is the most likely effect?
options: Frog numbers fall and insect numbers rise as the snakes are gone
Both frogs and insects vanish immediately
Frog numbers rise and insect numbers fall
questions.explain: Removing the predator reduces predation on frogs, so they increase and eat more insects. Insects therefore decline.
why_wrong: Frogs would not fall without their predator.
More frogs would eat more insects, not let them increase.
Immediate disappearance is not expected.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly shows a grazing food chain?
questions.explain: A grazing chain starts with a green plant, followed by a herbivore and then a carnivore. Grass to deer to tiger follows this order.
why_wrong: That chain starts with dead matter, so it is a detritus chain.
That reverses the direction of energy flow.
A herbivore cannot precede the plant it eats.

questions.q: In the ocean, tiny phytoplankton support a larger mass of zooplankton at a given moment. Which pyramid is inverted in this situation?
options: Pyramid of energy and biomass both
questions.explain: Phytoplankton reproduce very fast and are consumed quickly, so their standing biomass can be smaller than that of the consumers. Pyramids of energy remain upright.
why_wrong: Energy pyramids are never inverted.
Energy pyramids are always upright, so naming both is wrong.
The standing biomass pyramid is inverted here.

questions.q: Why is the pyramid of energy always upright in every ecosystem?
options: Producers are always fewer in number than the herbivores above them
Consumers are always larger in body size
Energy is lost as heat at each trophic level
questions.explain: Much of the energy at each level is lost in respiration and as heat, so less is available at successive levels.
why_wrong: Producers are not necessarily fewer, and that concerns numbers.
Body size does not govern energy transfer.
Decomposers do not store the energy.

questions.q: One large mango tree supports hundreds of insects that feed on it. What is the shape of the pyramid of numbers for the tree and the insects?
options: Inverted, since one producer supports many herbivores
Perfectly upright, because there are many producers at the base
Upright, since producers are always the most numerous in every ecosystem and nothing else
questions.explain: A single large producer supports many insects, so the base is narrower than the next level. The number pyramid is therefore inverted, not upright.
why_wrong: There is only one producer, so it is not upright with many producers.
That is a different kind of pyramid.
It can be drawn.

questions.q: Fresh lava cools to bare rock. Lichens arrive first and slowly form soil. What is this process called?
questions.explain: Primary succession starts on a surface with no soil or life. Lichens are pioneer species that begin soil formation.
why_wrong: Secondary succession starts where soil already exists.
Climax regression is not the process described.
Biomagnification is the build-up of toxins up a food chain.

questions.q: An abandoned farm field in Haryana turns into grass, then shrubs, then trees over some years. Why is this faster than succession on bare rock?
options: It has no soil at all, so succession is much slower
Soil and a seed bank already exist
questions.explain: This is secondary succession, which begins on land that still has soil and seeds. Primary succession must first create soil.
why_wrong: The field has soil, which is the key difference.
Seeds in the soil help regrowth.
Sunlight is available.

questions.q: A shallow pond fills with silt over decades and finally turns into a meadow and then forest. What is this type of succession called?
options: Xerarch succession, which starts on dry bare surfaces
Lithosere, which starts on bare rock
questions.explain: Hydrarch succession begins in water and proceeds towards land through submerged, floating and reed-swamp stages.
why_wrong: Xerarch succession begins on dry areas.
A lithosere starts on bare rock.
Climax regression is not a recognised stage of this type.

questions.q: Where a forest meets a grassland, a biologist records more species than in either interior. What explains this?
options: Biomagnification of toxins in the food chain
Eutrophication of the nearby water body
Bioaccumulation of toxins inside one organism
The edge effect in the ecotone
questions.explain: An ecotone shares species of both neighbouring communities and its own, giving higher diversity. This is the edge effect.
why_wrong: Biomagnification concerns toxins in food chains.
Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of water.
Bioaccumulation is toxin build-up in an organism.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-renewable resource that is NOT a fossil fuel?
questions.explain: Uranium is a mineral fuel for nuclear reactors and cannot be replaced once mined. Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels formed from ancient organisms.
why_wrong: Natural gas is a fossil fuel.
Coal is a fossil fuel.
Petroleum is a fossil fuel.

questions.q: A forest is harvested exactly as fast as it regrows. Which statement best describes the use of this resource?
options: Sustainable use of a renewable resource
questions.explain: Renewable resources stay available when the harvest does not exceed the regeneration rate. That is the meaning of sustainable use.
why_wrong: Forests are renewable, not non-renewable.
If harvest equals regrowth, the stock is not depleted.
Forests do not convert into fossil resources by this practice.

questions.q: Which statement correctly joins energy flow and nutrient cycling in an ecosystem?
options: Both energy and nutrients are recycled endlessly within the ecosystem
Energy is recycled by decomposers while nutrients flow one way and are never reused
Neither energy nor nutrients are lost from the system
Energy flows one way and is lost as heat, while nutrients are recycled
questions.explain: Energy enters as sunlight, passes along trophic levels and is dissipated as heat, so it cannot be reused. Nutrients circulate between organisms and the environment.
why_wrong: Energy is not recycled.
The roles are reversed in this statement.
Energy is steadily lost as heat.

questions.q: Which statement about ecological pyramids is INCORRECT?
options: The pyramid of energy can be inverted in a pond
The pyramid of biomass can be inverted in the ocean
The pyramid of numbers can be inverted in a parasitic chain
The pyramid of energy is always upright
questions.explain: Energy pyramids are never inverted because energy is lost at each step. Biomass and number pyramids can be inverted in some ecosystems.
why_wrong: This is true because of fast-growing phytoplankton.
This is true because one host can carry many parasites.
This is a correct statement.

questions.q: In a parasitic food chain, such as one tree hosting many insects that carry many parasites, what is the usual shape of the pyramid of numbers?
options: Always spindle-shaped with a sharp tip
questions.explain: Each level has more individuals than the one below it, as parasites outnumber hosts. This gives an inverted number pyramid.
why_wrong: Numbers increase upward here, so it is not upright.
Rectangular would mean equal numbers.
Numbers do not narrow to a tip in this chain.

questions.q: As succession moves towards the climax community, how does the ratio of gross production to community respiration (P/R) generally change?
options: It remains much greater than ten
questions.explain: In young communities production exceeds respiration. At climax, production and respiration balance, giving a ratio close to one.
why_wrong: A ratio far above one marks the early stages, not the climax.
Zero would mean no production.
A high ratio is characteristic of immature communities.

questions.q: Which statement about succession is correct?
options: Secondary succession begins on land that has lost its community but kept soil
Primary succession begins on land that already has rich soil and seeds
Pioneer species appear last in a succession, after the climax community has formed
The climax community is the first stage
questions.explain: Secondary succession occurs after disturbance such as fire or abandonment, where soil survives. Primary succession starts on bare surfaces.
why_wrong: Primary succession starts on bare rock or similar sites without soil.
Pioneer species are the first colonisers.
The climax community is the final stage.

questions.q: The Aral Sea shrank greatly mainly because its feeder rivers were diverted. For what purpose was most of the water diverted?
questions.explain: Water from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya was diverted for large-scale irrigation, mostly of cotton. It is a standard example of surface water overuse.
why_wrong: The main diversion was not for reactor cooling.
Coal washing did not use most of the river flow.
Hydrogen production was not the reason.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical effect of a large dam?
options: Submergence of land, forest and farmland under the reservoir
Greater silt delivery to the downstream delta
questions.explain: Dams trap sediment in the reservoir, so less silt reaches the delta. The other options are recognised effects.
why_wrong: Submergence of land is a standard effect.
Displacement is a major social impact.
Reservoir-induced seismicity is a recognised concern.

questions.q: Which of the following is a soil conservation method and NOT a cause of soil erosion?
options: Ploughing up and down a slope
questions.explain: Contour ploughing follows the slope's contours and slows runoff. The other options expose soil or speed water flow.
why_wrong: Overgrazing removes ground cover.
Deforestation removes protective roots.
This lets water run straight downhill.

questions.q: A city covers its land with roads and buildings. Which two resources are affected together?
options: Wind energy and tidal energy of the nearby coast
Uranium and thorium reserves of the area
questions.explain: Impervious surfaces cut infiltration, which lowers groundwater recharge while changing land use. It links land and water resources.
why_wrong: Paved surfaces do not directly change wind or tidal energy.
Mineral fuels are not affected by paving.
Gas fuels are unrelated to paving.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches a land degradation process with a condition that causes it?
options: Waterlogging and salinity with over-irrigation and poor drainage
Desertification with heavy rainfall over dense, undisturbed forest cover
Landslide on flat arid land with sparse vegetation
Soil erosion with thick plant cover
questions.explain: Too much irrigation without drainage lifts the water table and brings salts up. The other pairs are mismatched.
why_wrong: Desertification occurs where vegetation is lost in dry areas.
Landslides occur on steep slopes.
Thick plant cover protects soil from erosion.

questions.q: Deforestation of a large catchment affects both rainfall and the atmosphere. Which pair of effects is correct?
options: More transpiration and a lower level of carbon dioxide
More groundwater recharge and more oxygen
Less transpiration and a rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide
Higher humidity and less carbon dioxide in the air above the catchment
questions.explain: Fewer trees mean less water vapour returned to the air and less carbon absorbed, while burning and decay release carbon dioxide.
why_wrong: Fewer trees reduce transpiration and carbon uptake.
Deforestation reduces infiltration and photosynthetic oxygen.
Humidity falls and carbon dioxide does not.

questions.q: Why can a monoculture timber plantation not fully replace a natural forest?
options: It produces more oxygen than any natural forest can ever give
It supports far fewer species and ecosystem functions
It recharges groundwater more than natural forest
questions.explain: Single-species plantations lack the layers and diversity of natural forests. Their wildlife support and resilience are lower.
why_wrong: There is no basis for that claim.
Natural forests generally regulate water better.
Plantations usually need intensive management.

questions.q: What is the main combustible component of biogas?
questions.explain: Biogas from anaerobic digestion of organic waste is mostly methane with carbon dioxide. Methane gives it fuel value.
why_wrong: Carbon monoxide is not the main component.
Hydrogen sulphide is only a minor impurity.
Ammonia is not the main gas.

questions.q: How does a solar photovoltaic cell differ from a solar thermal collector?
options: Both only store heat in water tanks and neither produces any electricity at all
The photovoltaic cell works only at night
The collector turns sunlight directly into electricity, while the cell only gathers heat
The cell turns sunlight directly into electricity; the collector gathers heat
questions.explain: Photovoltaic cells use the photoelectric effect to produce electric current. Thermal collectors absorb solar radiation as heat.
why_wrong: Photovoltaic cells produce electricity, not stored heat.
Photovoltaic cells need light and do not work at night.
The roles are reversed in this statement.

questions.q: Ocean thermal energy conversion works by exploiting which difference?
options: The difference in salinity between rivers and deserts of the region
The temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep water
The speed of wind over land
The difference in height between high and low tide
questions.explain: OTEC uses warm surface water to vaporise a working fluid and cold deep water to condense it, driving a turbine.
why_wrong: Salinity differences are not what OTEC uses.
Wind speed is for wind turbines.
Tidal height is used in tidal power.

questions.q: Firewood is renewable, yet a hill district runs short of fuelwood. What best explains this apparent contradiction?
options: Wood stops being a biological resource once it is cut and collected
Harvesting is faster than regrowth, so the renewable stock declines
Fuelwood is a non-renewable mineral resource like coal that cannot regrow
questions.explain: A renewable resource can be exhausted if its use exceeds natural renewal. Fuelwood is renewable only when the rate of cutting is below regrowth.
why_wrong: Wood remains a biological resource.
Coal forms over millions of years, not quickly.
Wood is not a mineral.

questions.q: Which individual habit helps conserve both water and energy at once?
options: Leaving taps running while brushing and using a geyser for long periods
Using a bucket and taking shorter showers with a solar heater
questions.explain: Using less hot water saves the water itself and the energy used to heat it. The other habits waste one or both.
why_wrong: Running taps wastes water.
An always-on geyser wastes energy.
Half loads waste both water and power.

questions.q: Which organisms at deep-sea hydrothermal vents act as producers although there is no sunlight?
questions.explain: These bacteria oxidise chemicals such as hydrogen sulphide to make food. Producers therefore include chemosynthetic as well as photosynthetic organisms.
why_wrong: Algae need sunlight to photosynthesise.
Fungi are decomposers.
Zooplankton are consumers.

questions.q: Which organism physically fragments dead leaves, making them easier for decomposers to act on?
questions.explain: Detritivores ingest and break dead matter into smaller pieces, increasing surface area for microbial decomposition. Fungi then digest it chemically.
why_wrong: Fungi decompose chemically by secreting enzymes rather than fragmenting physically.
Grass is a producer.
A hawk does not feed on leaf litter.

questions.q: Which pair correctly classifies the ecosystem types?
options: River is lentic and pond is lotic
River is lotic and pond is lentic
Both river and pond are lentic
Both river and pond are lotic ecosystems
questions.explain: Lotic ecosystems have running water, such as rivers and streams, while lentic ones have still water, such as ponds and lakes.
why_wrong: The terms are reversed here.
A river has running water so it is not lentic.
A pond has standing water so it is not lotic.

questions.q: Per unit area, which of these ecosystems typically has the lowest productivity?
questions.explain: Nutrient-poor open ocean has low productivity per unit area. Rainforests, estuaries and reefs are among the most productive.
why_wrong: Tropical rainforest is highly productive.
Estuaries are very productive.
Coral reefs are very productive.

questions.q: With about ten percent transfer between levels, what fraction of the producer energy reaches the fifth trophic level?
questions.explain: There are four transfers from level one to level five, so the fraction is 0.1 to the power four, which is 0.0001 or 0.01 percent.
why_wrong: 0.1 percent would be three transfers.
1 percent would be two transfers.
10 percent would be a single transfer.

questions.q: Pesticide residue is found in a hawk at a far higher concentration than in the grass and insects below it. Which process explains this?
options: Photosynthesis in the grass that feeds the insects
questions.explain: Persistent toxins accumulate in tissues and increase in concentration at each trophic level. Top predators carry the highest amounts.
why_wrong: Succession is a change in community over time.
Photosynthesis makes food and does not concentrate toxins.
Nitrogen fixation makes nitrogen available to plants.

questions.q: Why is a food web generally more stable than a single food chain?
options: Each consumer eats only one species, so a loss has no knock-on effect
Consumers have alternative food sources if one species declines
It has fewer species and fewer feeding links than a single chain
questions.explain: Many cross-links let predators switch prey, so the loss of one species does not collapse the system.
why_wrong: Single-prey dependence would make the web fragile.
Energy is not recycled.
Webs have more species and links.

questions.q: In the Y-shaped energy flow model, what do the two arms of the Y represent?
options: Biotic and abiotic components of the ecosystem, respectively
The grazing and detritus food chains
questions.explain: Energy from the sun enters and then splits into the grazing chain and the detritus chain, which begin from living and dead matter respectively.
why_wrong: The two arms are food chains and not just those groups.
The model describes chains within an ecosystem.
The arms describe pathways of energy flow.

questions.q: In a typical grassland, what is the usual shape of the pyramid of numbers?
questions.explain: Many grass plants support fewer herbivores, which support still fewer carnivores. This produces an upright pyramid.
why_wrong: Inverted shapes arise with a single large producer or parasites.
Spindle shapes arise in some tree ecosystems.
Numbers clearly decrease up the levels.

questions.q: A hostel resident notices that the corridor lights and fans stay on all night in empty rooms. Which individual action best conserves energy?
options: Leaving them on so that they do not wear out from repeated switching
Switching off lights and fans when leaving a room
Writing a complaint but changing no habits
questions.explain: Energy saved at the point of use directly lowers demand on power stations. Small habits repeated by many individuals add up to large savings.
why_wrong: Running appliances unnecessarily wastes electricity and does not protect them.
Higher wattage raises consumption.
Complaining alone saves no energy.

questions.q: A pond has abundant algae but its bottom is full of dead leaves that are not decaying because the bacteria and fungi were killed by a chemical spill. What is the most likely result?
options: Nutrients stay locked in dead matter and recycling slows
Energy begins to flow in a cycle
Producers gain extra minerals from the dead leaves at once
questions.explain: Decomposers release nutrients from dead matter for reuse by producers. Without them, nutrients stay tied up and cycling slows.
why_wrong: Cycling slows when decomposers die.
Energy flow is one-way and never cyclic.
Dead leaves cannot supply minerals unless decomposed.

questions.q: Which statement about the climax community is correct?
options: It is relatively stable and in balance with the climate of the area
It is the first stage of succession and has the lowest species diversity
It always has more annual herbs than trees
It keeps changing quickly into the pioneer stage
questions.explain: The climax is the final, self-perpetuating stage of succession, in equilibrium with climate. It remains stable unless disturbed.
why_wrong: The pioneer community is the first stage.
Climax communities in forest regions are typically dominated by trees.
Rapid change is characteristic of early stages.

questions.q: Which is the correct statement about trophic levels?
options: Each species occupies only one fixed trophic level in every chain
Producers are always at the top trophic level
Decomposers always form the first trophic level in every ecosystem and chain
A species may occupy different trophic levels in different food chains
questions.explain: Omnivores such as humans can be primary consumers in one chain and secondary in another. So the trophic level depends on the chain.
why_wrong: Many omnivores change level between chains.
Producers occupy the first level.
Producers, not decomposers, form the first level.
